note: A butcher was suspected of selling the forbidden fat near the kidney as permitted intestinal fat. Rava penalized him by forbidding him to sell even nuts. Rav Pappa asked whether Rava was following the stricter view, in which case he should forbid even water and salt. Rava explained that the penalty was tied to the offense itself: the butcher had used nuts, which children love, to lure butchers' children into bringing him the forbidden fat, which he then sold as permitted.
why: The mishna has just set out a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says one may buy nothing at all from a suspect seller, and Rabbi Shimon says only items connected to his offense are barred. Rava shows his ruling fits Rabbi Shimon.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who penalizes the butcher.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who questions which opinion Rava's penalty follows.

terms.meaning: Certain fats of cattle, sheep and goats, such as the fat around the kidneys, that the Torah forbids to be eaten, while other fat is permitted.

note: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reported in the name of Rabbi Meir an incident about a woman who was married to a haver and would tie his phylacteries on his hand. Later she married a tax collector, and she would tie tax seals on his hand.
why: The Sages are debating whether the household of a haver who move into the home of someone less observant must formally take on the haver's commitments again; Rabbi Meir says they must, and the incident shows how fully a wife's practice follows her husband.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Sage who holds that even these people must take on the commitments, and in whose name the incident is told.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

terms.meaning: A member of a fellowship devoted to careful observance, especially of ritual purity and tithes.
Tefillin: leather boxes holding Torah verses, bound on the arm and head during prayer.
Marks or tokens a tax collector wore, here bound on the hand where phylacteries had been.

note: Rav Sheshet was troubled by a problem one night and solved it in the morning from a baraita. His attendant, Rav Idi, heard the solution from him and repeated it in the study hall without saying it was Rav Sheshet's. When Rav Sheshet heard, he was annoyed and said: the one who stung me, let him be stung by a scorpion.
why: The Gemara has found a contradiction over whether the meat of an animal tithe may be sold, which Rav Sheshet resolved. It explains his anger with Rav's teaching that David prayed for his words to be quoted in his name: a scholar quoted by name moves his lips in the grave.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A Sage who solves a legal problem overnight and is angered when his answer is repeated without his name.

people.name: Rav Idi
people.about: Rav Sheshet's attendant, who repeats the solution in the study hall without crediting him.

people.name: David
people.about: King David, who according to Rav asked God that people repeat his teachings in his name after his death.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
Every tenth newborn animal of the herd, which is consecrated; its meat may normally not be sold.
The place where the Sages and their students gathered to learn and debate.
